newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS-Hungary sees lower interest rates,stable C/A.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hungary sees lower interest rates,stable C/A.

text.p: Hungary's cut in its planned devaluation rate and central bank base rate, plus an upgrade by a credit rating agency, reflect expectations for a decline in interest rates and a stable current account, analysts said on Tuesday.
Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy said the rate of the monthly forint devaluations would be cut to one percent on August 15 from the current 1.1 percent.
"Everybody expects interest rates to go down," said Peter Muszely of Concorde Securities. "(The devaluation rate cut) is seen as a very justified and conservative decision.
"It will not jeopardise the foreign trade balance, even together with the abolition of the three percent customs surcharge on July 1," said Budapest Bank's Peter Bihari.

The announcement coincided with Hungary's upgrading by credit rating agency IBCA to BBB from BBB-minus and a 0.5 percent cut in the National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) base rate to 21 percent, effective on July 1.
Reacting to the news, the Budapest Stock Exchange shrugged off Wall Street's 2.5 percent plunge on Monday and soared to a record high of 6,597.28 points, up by 1.67 percent.

Analysts said the changes reflected an improvement in Hungary's external accounts and inflation. National Bank of Hungary President Gyorgy Suranyi told Reuters that Hungary's upgrading by IBCA underscored the country's economic progress.

The analysts said a change in the NBH base rate usually had little impact on the markets but together with the devaluation rate cut it indicated expectations for a moderate decline in interest rates and a stable foreign trade account balance.

They said the government chose the best time for the announcement of the devaluation cut, as recently reported March trade and current account deficit and inflation figures were good but the next two months would show some rise in inflation.
"We have had the good news now and the government could make this new step," said New York Broker's Zoltan Bereczki.

In June and July, year-on-year inflation was likely to rise, the first time since January 1996, due to low seasonal good prices in the comparative period of 1996 and gas retail hikes of 11.3 percent on average and electricity price increases of 4.5 on July 1, analysts said.
"However, after August I expect a decline (in inflation) again," said Laszlo Batora.
"Apparently the government wanted to help the further decline in inflation with the devaluation rate cut," Bereczki said.

The devaluation rate cut, agreed by the government and the NBH, fit in with a set of recent decisions by the central bank, including a 0.5 percent cut in repo rates two weeks ago and the abolition of the six-month and 12-month NBH deposit facilities last week, analysts said.

The reduction in the devaluation rate -- the so-called crawling peg devaluator -- opened the way for a 20 to 30 basis point fall in government securities yields, which stalled in the past three months following the launch of a 12-month NBH deposit facility, they added.

However, one-year government securities were likely to drop little until the NBH cuts the 20.25 percent yield of its own one-month bonds, first issued last Friday, analysts said, adding that after probable falls in the next few days interest rates were likely to drop only slowly later this year.
The government indicated with the 10 basis point devaluation cut that it did not want a too quick decline in interest rates, analysts said.
However, some believe the cut could have been more radical and a 20 basis point reduction would not have been surprising.

Concorde Securities analyst Peter Muszely said the government may have been cautious as according to NBH figures the real value of the net increase in household savings dropped by 13.6 percent in January-April from the same period in 1996.

However, the NBH registered only savings placed with banks, while savings in stocks have substantially risen in the past eighteen months, with the index of the Budapest Stock Exchange rising by more than 300 percent, he said.

"According to our estimations, household savings rose by more than 200 billion forints in the first four months, rather than 176 billion as the NBH said," he said, adding that this was a three to four percent rise in real terms.

He added that the devaluation cut decision was unlikely to jeopardise Hungary's exports, with a 2.5 percent forecast economic growth along with a projected two percent drop in the number of employed was likely to improve productivity.
